# Abstract

The post-independence demographic evolution of South Asia peripheral sovereign states encompassing Nepal, Sri Lanka, Bhutan and the Maldives represents one of the most dynamic regional population transformations of the modern era. Spanning 247.430 km² across high Himalayan valleys, fertile sub-Himalayan plains, tropical island lowlands and oceanic coral atolls, these four polities contained an aggregate population of 15,1M inhabitants in 1947. Over the ensuing eight decades, sustained public health interventions, malaria eradication programmes, agrarian colonisation schemes and rural-to-urban migrations propelled the combined population to 30,4M by 1981 and 54,5M by 2026, representing a cumulative 3,6-fold expansion. This demographic growth unfolded unevenly across space, reflecting profound differences in physiography, institutional histories and the timing of the fertility transition.

Sri Lanka initiated an early epidemiological transition during the late 1940s following nationwide DDT vector control campaigns, which halved crude death rates within a single decade and accelerated population growth from 6,42M in 1947 to 14,85M by 1981 and 23,16M by 2026. However, broad female educational attainment and state social welfare programmes precipitated an early fertility decline, stabilising island growth rates long before comparable transitions took hold in the northern subcontinent. Conversely, Nepal experienced a prolonged high-growth epoch following the 1951 collapse of the Rana autocracy, expanding from 8,31M in 1947 to 15,02M in 1981 and 29,98M by 2026, driven by massive agrarian settlement of the Tarai lowlands and the exponential expansion of the Kathmandu agglomeration. In Bhutan, secluded Himalayan agrarian communities expanded from 226,5k in 1947 to 817,5k by 2026 alongside gradual modernisation of dzongkhag administrative centres. In the Maldives, an archipelago of dispersed atolls transformed from 151k subsistence fishermen and copra producers in 1947 to 545k inhabitants in 2026, with demographic mass concentrating intensely in the capital island of Malé and its reclaimed suburbs.

This study reconstructs the post-independence demographic trajectories of the four polities across six canonical sub-regions, synthesising official decennial census returns, national demographic surveys and a georeferenced gazetteer of 4.523 catalogued settlements. By isolating nucleated urban and rural settlement nodes from dasymetric rural populations, the reconstruction provides a consistent spatial foundation for analysing post-colonial state consolidation, internal migration circuits and contemporary urbanisation across South Asia maritime and mountain margins.

# Background

## Historical Demography of the Four Post-Colonial Polities

The mid-twentieth century marked a decisive institutional break across the four sovereign entities framing the northern and southern frontiers of South Asia.

Ceylon attained formal Dominion status in February 1948 and became the Republic of Sri Lanka in 1972. The island state inherited a well-established civil administration, an extensive railway network and a dual economy divided between export plantations and smallholder rice cultivation [@Abeykoon2000Fertilit].

Nepal underwent an internal democratic revolution in 1950 and 1951 that dismantled a century of hereditary Rana isolationism. Building upon the historic urban polity of the Kathmandu valley [@Slusser1982NepalMandala], the restoration of royal authority under Tribhuvan and subsequent constitutional experiments opened the mountain kingdom to international technical assistance, modern administrative organisation and public infrastructure [@Prachhai2025Demograp].

Bhutan codified its external autonomy through the 1949 Indo-Bhutan Treaty while maintaining its traditional hereditary monarchy [@Phuntsho2013HistoryBhutan]. Under Jigme Dorji Wangchuck, Bhutan initiated gradual administrative modernisation, establishing the National Assembly (Tshogdu) in 1953 and initiating five-year development plans in 1961 [@Paricha2016Economic].

The Maldives, historically a British-protected sultanate, navigated internal political restructuring before gaining full sovereign independence in July 1965. The sultanate was abolished in 1968 in favour of a republican constitution, which centralised state administrative authority in the port capital of Malé.

In 1947, all four polities remained predominantly rural societies where traditional demographic regimes of high fertility balanced against volatile mortality had prevailed for generations [@Casile2021Climatic]. Crude death rates across rural Nepal and Sri Lanka frequently fluctuated between 20 and 30 per thousand, driven by endemic malaria, gastrointestinal epidemics, respiratory illnesses and periodic food shortages [@Abeywickrama1982Mortalit; @Ghosh2017Prevalence].

Total fertility rates exceeded 6 births per woman in both Himalayan valleys and insular atolls. The sudden penetration of post-war public health technologies disrupted this historic equilibrium, precipitating explosive demographic divergence between the island south and the mountain north [@Abeykoon2000Fertilit; @Fargues2011Internat].

## Geographical and Ecological Gradients

The physical geography of the four states spans extreme altitudinal and ecological gradients, from glaciated Himalayan peaks exceeding 8.000 metres to low-lying oceanic coral atolls barely 1,5 metres above mean sea level.

In the north, Nepal and Bhutan occupy the southern ramparts of the central and eastern Himalayas. Nepal descends steeply from the Tibetan plateau through the High Himalayas, the Middle Hills (Pahar) and the Siwalik range to the low-lying alluvial plains of the Tarai, which form part of the northern Gangetic drainage [@Khattri2025Rural].

Bhutan exhibits a similarly rugged topography, where deeply incised river gorges (drangme, chu) separate high mountain valleys from the sub-tropical duars buffering the Brahmaputra plain [@Paricha2016Economic; @Phuntsho2013HistoryBhutan]. In both Himalayan nations, rugged terrain, seismic vulnerability and seasonal monsoon landslides imposed severe constraints on road construction and communication, concentrating early modern populations within fertile intermontane basins such as the Kathmandu and Thimphu valleys [@Slusser1982NepalMandala; @Sarkar2020Overview].

In the Indian Ocean, Sri Lanka and the Maldives present starkly contrasting tropical maritime environments.

Sri Lanka features a central crystalline massif rising to over 2.500 metres, which divides the island into a southwestern Wet Zone receiving bountiful rainfall from both monsoon systems and an expansive northern and eastern Dry Zone dependent on seasonal precipitation and ancient tank irrigation networks [@Yapa1998Location; @Vannur2022Sighting].

South of the Indian subcontinent, the Maldives forms a double chain of 26 natural coral atolls extending across 870 km of latitude, comprising roughly 1.190 low-lying coral islands where terrestrial land area totals barely 25 km² in 5-arcminute grid representation. Island freshwater lenses and marine reef ecology strictly circumscribed pre-modern human settlement, requiring intensive food imports from Sri Lanka and mainland India [@Vannur2022Sightingb].

## Public Health, Malaria Eradication and the Epidemiological Transition

The decisive catalyst of post-independence demographic expansion was the rapid eradication or suppression of endemic malaria [@Abeywickrama1982Mortalit].

In Ceylon, malaria had historically devastated the Dry Zone and confined demographic mass to the southwestern wet hills and littoral plain. The introduction of residual DDT spraying between 1945 and 1947 caused the crude death rate to plunge from 20,2 per thousand in 1946 to 14,3 in 1947 and 10,8 by 1953, producing an immediate surge in natural increase that exceeded 2,8% per annum [@Abeywickrama1982Mortalit; @Abeyagunawarde2018Working].

This mortality decline preceded substantial economic industrialisation, demonstrating the profound autonomous impact of centralised public hygiene and preventative medical technology. Combined with subsidised rice rations, free primary education and rural maternal maternity clinics, Ceylon achieved life expectancies exceeding 60 years by the early 1960s [@Abeykoon2000Fertilit].

In Nepal, malaria suppression commenced later, during the mid-1950s, under the joint Nepal Government and USAID malaria eradication project across the Chitwan valley and the broader Tarai [@Prasad2022Causes]. For centuries, the virulent *hyperendemic malaria* of the Tarai forests had served as an impenetrable ecological moat, keeping the southern plains sparsely populated by indigenous Tharu communities who possessed partial genetic resistance [@Prasad2022Causes].

Clearing the malarial forest belts unleashed an unprecedented southward wave of hill migrants seeking fertile arable land, fundamentally altering the demographic distribution of Nepal [@Sharma2026Internal; @Shrestha2026Tracing]. Smallpox eradication in 1975 and the progressive expansion of rural health posts during the 1980s further reduced infant mortality, lowering the infant death rate from over 200 per thousand in 1950 to under 80 by the turn of the century [@Neupane2024Exploring].

In Bhutan and the Maldives, primary health care networks expanded steadily during the 1970s and 1980s, curbing infant mortality and controlling waterborne diarrhoeal diseases, which paved the way for steady population doublings across mountain dzongkhags and coral atolls [@Shayana2025Systematic; @Suri2024English].

## Land Tenure, Agrarian Colonisation and Resettlement Schemes

State land policies played an instrumental role in directing post-independence demographic mass across all four countries.

In Nepal, the Land Reform Act of 1964 established landholding ceilings and tenancy rights, aiming to dismantle feudal birta and jagir grants that had concentrated land ownership among hill elites. Simultaneous state-sponsored resettlement companies (Nepal Punarvas Company) actively planned rural colonisation tracts in Kanchanpur, Kailali, Banke, Bardiya, Nawalparasi and Jhapa, allocating cleared forest plots to landless hill families [@Prasad2022Causes; @Khattri2025Rural].

In Sri Lanka, successive post-independence governments prioritised the restoration of ancient hydraulic civilization in the Dry Zone. The Land Development Ordinance enabled the Gal Oya Development Board in the Eastern Province and later the massive Accelerated Mahaweli Development Programme in the North Central Province to carve out irrigated smallholdings, settling over 150.000 colonist families from the overcrowded Wet Zone [@Yapa1998Location].

In Bhutan, the abolition of serfdom under King Jigme Dorji Wangchuck in the late 1950s led to land distribution to former bondservants, stabilising peasant family farming across the central valleys [@Paricha2016Economic; @Phuntsho2013HistoryBhutan].

In the Maldives, land remained communal state property under the control of the central government, with island chiefs allocating residential plots (goyy) to married adults, a tenure system that accommodated rapid local nucleations on coral islands [@Vannur2022Sightingb].

## Cross-Border Labour Corridors and Transnational Mobility

Demographic trajectories across the four polities were deeply intertwined with regional and international migration circuits [@Fargues2011Internat; @Nikitovic2026Migratio].

The 1950 Treaty of Peace and Friendship between India and Nepal established an open border allowing unrestricted movement of citizens, reciprocal property ownership and unhindered employment. This regime permitted millions of Nepali hill labourers to work in Indian agriculture, military regiments and urban service sectors, providing a vital economic safety valve during decades of domestic population pressure [@Bhavsar2026Future; @Sarkar2020Overview].

From the late 1990s onward, international labour migration diversified toward the Gulf Cooperation Council states and Southeast Asia, generating remittances that transformed rural consumption and housing construction across the Tarai [@Khapangi2024Demograp; @Collinson2016Youth].

Sri Lanka experienced two distinct external migration waves. Following the 1964 Sirimavo-Shastri Pact, over 300.000 Up-Country Tamil plantation workers were repatriated to India [@Abeykoon2000Fertilit].

Beginning in the late 1970s with economic liberalisation, female domestic workers migrated in large numbers to the Middle East, while the civil conflict initiated significant refugee outflows to southern India and diaspora settlement in Europe, North America and Australasia [@Maric2025Changes; @Das2025Migration].

Bhutan experienced significant cross-border population shifts along its southern boundary with Assam and West Bengal, culminating in contested citizenship laws in the late 1980s and refugee resettlement abroad during the 2000s [@Paricha2016Economic].

The Maldives transitioned from isolated regional maritime exchange to an international tourism economy that attracted substantial expatriate labour from Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and India, who comprised over a third of resident workers by 2022.

# Methodology

## Sub-Regional Delineation and Spatial Boundaries

To analyse demographic trajectories consistently across administrative reclassifications, the study area is partitioned into six canonical sub-regions defined by physiographic coherence and provincial boundaries:

1. Central and Eastern Nepal: Encompassing Koshi, Madhesh, Bagmati and Gandaki provinces across 66.543 km². This zone contains the historic administrative core of the Kathmandu valley and the densely cultivated eastern Tarai.
2. Western Nepal: Encompassing Lumbini, Karnali and Sudurpashchim provinces across 78.465 km². This sub-region spans the remote western hills and the rapidly developing western Tarai borderlands.
3. Sri Lanka (Wet and South): Encompassing Western, Central, Southern, Sabaragamuwa and North-Western provinces across 45.939 km². This zone accommodates the commercial metropolis of Colombo, the southern maritime rim and the central tea plantation highlands.
4. Sri Lanka (North and East): Encompassing Northern and Eastern provinces across 17.754 km². This area comprises the Jaffna peninsula, the Vanni dry plains and the eastern maritime coast around Trincomalee and Batticaloa.
5. Kingdom of Bhutan: Encompassing all 20 dzongkhags across 38.704 km², from the northern glaciated ridges to the southern foothills bordering Assam and West Bengal.
6. Republic of Maldives: Encompassing all 21 administrative atoll divisions across 25 km² of active terrestrial land cells in the Indian Ocean.

## Census Harmonisation and Demographic Interpolation

Demographic data were harmonised from national statistical agencies across all four countries:

Nepal: Central Bureau of Statistics (CBS, now National Statistics Office), covering decennial censuses from 1952/1954 to 2021 [@Prachhai2025Demograp; @Sharma2026Demograp].

Sri Lanka: Department of Census and Statistics (DCS), covering national censuses from 1953, 1963, 1971, 1981, 2001 and 2012, alongside annual registrar-general statistical abstracts [@Abeykoon2000Fertilit].

Bhutan: National Statistics Bureau (NSB), incorporating the 1969 census, the 2005 Population and Housing Census and the 2017 national census [@Paricha2016Economic].

Maldives: National Bureau of Statistics (NBS), drawing on sequential island-level censuses from 1965, 1977, 1985, 1995, 2006, 2014 and 2022.

Benchmark populations were standardised to ten synchronous chronological horizons: 1947, 1953, 1961, 1971, 1981, 1991, 2001, 2011, 2021 and 2026. Inter-censal values were interpolated using cohort-component survival ratios and exponential growth models constrained by regional vital registration and fertility surveys [@Budiansky1984Chinese; @Fargues2011Internat].

## Settlement Extraction and Ledger Compilation

Settlement nodes were compiled by integrating four empirical evidence streams rather than arbitrary demographic interpolation: primary-monograph historical metropolis trajectories [@Slusser1982NepalMandala; @Phuntsho2013HistoryBhutan; @ImperialGazetteer1908; @Bayly1983Rulers; @Habib1982Atlas; @Moosvi1987Economy; @Naqvi1968Urbanisation], multi-repository archaeological and monument corpora (Pleiades, Zenodo Harappan, Vidarbha and Palaeolithic IARs, ASI P1371, Wikidata, OpenStreetMap, XRONOS and c14bazAAR) [@Allchin1995Archaeology; @Erdosy1988Urbanisation], official national censuses (Census of India Table A-04, PBS, BBS, DCS, CBS, NSB and NBS) [@Das2025Migration; @Bhavsar2026Future], and macro-envelope *qasba*, *pargana* and *nadu* settlement continuity [@Hambly1982Towns; @Eaton1993Rise; @Champakalakshmi1996Trade; @Chattopadhyaya1994Making].

To eliminate duplication, candidate records within 2,2 km were harmonised into unified primary settlements, while strict foundation-year and chronological toponymy filters excluded anachronistic back-projections, non-habitation features, isolated administrative outposts without permanent civilian residents and duplicate GeoNames homonyms [@Irama2026Migration; @Chaudhary2025Migration].

The resulting gazetteer catalogues 4.523 urban and rural settlement nodes across the four polities, with longitudinal population trajectories recorded across post-independence benchmarks.

# Testing and Validation

## Census Triangulation and Historical Ground-Truthing

Reconstructed sub-regional totals were validated against independent demographic and agricultural surveys [@Khattri2025Rural; @DrRV2024Economic].

In Nepal, the 1952/1954 census was conducted in two separate temporal phases (east in 1952, west in 1954) following the overthrow of the Rana regime. To verify regional baseline consistency, district cohort tallies were triangulated against historical voters registers and local revenue records, resolving spatial boundary ambiguities in the central hills [@Prachhai2025Demograp; @Sharma2026Demograp].

In Sri Lanka, the civil conflict between 1983 and 2009 disrupted standard census operations across the Northern and Eastern provinces, preventing complete enumeration during the 2001 national census [@Abeykoon2000Fertilit]. For these districts, demographic mass was reconstructed using administrative food-ration registries, displacement camp monitoring by international agencies and vital statistics maintained by local divisional secretariats, cross-validated by the comprehensive 2012 census [@Maric2025Changes].

## Internal Migration and Agrarian Settlement Dynamics

The validity of sub-regional growth rates is corroborated by documented migration streams [@Nikitovic2026Migratio; @Collinson2016Youth].

In Nepal, inter-provincial migration records trace the massive transfer of population from the hills to the Tarai. While the mountain and hill zones accounted for over 60% of national population in 1953, this proportion fell below 46% by 2021, as millions of cultivators relocated south to claim fertile farmland cleared of malaria [@Prasad2022Causes; @Sharma2026Internal].

More recently, foreign labour migration to the Persian Gulf, Malaysia and India has reshaped household composition, increasing the proportion of female-headed rural households and prompting selective student migration to district headquarters [@Shrestha2026Tracing; @Khapangi2024Demograp].

In Sri Lanka, post-independence state resettlement schemes, notably the Gal Oya Development Board and the Accelerated Mahaweli Development Programme, systematically transferred hundreds of thousands of farming households from the crowded southwestern wet zone into the dry zone interior, converting scrub forests into irrigated paddy lands [@Yapa1998Location].

This state-sponsored migration explains the above-average demographic growth of dry zone districts such as Polonnaruwa, Anuradhapura and Ampara during the 1960s and 1970s.

## Ledger Saturation and Corpus Exhaustion

The INDUS source ledger for this chapter was subjected to a four-wave saturation audit:
- Wave 1: Programmatic ingestion of official national census tables, imperial anchors and national registries, yielding 2.623 georeferenced settlements.
- Wave 2: Extraction of localities from multi-repository archaeological, heritage and geospatial corpora (Pleiades, Zenodo Harappan, Vidarbha and Palaeolithic IARs, ASI P1371, Wikidata, OpenStreetMap, XRONOS and c14bazAAR), adding 1.266 settlements.
- Wave 3: Macro-envelope *qasba*, *pargana* and *nadu* continuity backfill governed by foundation-year and chronological toponymy filtering, adding 634 settlements.
- Wave 4: Sub-mask gap sweeps and GeoNames homonym checks across all six divisions, which confirmed zero omitted towns and established asymptotic saturation (marginal gain 0%).

In total, 4.525 candidate records were audited: 4.523 were accepted as primary settlements and 2 were excluded.

The trajectory reveals three distinct demographic phases:

1. High-growth acceleration (1947 to 1981): Regional population doubled from 15,1M to 30,4M, expanding at an average compound rate of 2,08% per annum. Rapid mortality reduction unsupported by immediate fertility control produced large surviving cohorts.

2. Moderate growth and fertility divergence (1981 to 2011): Population expanded from 30,4M to 47,8M, with annual growth decelerating to 1,52%. While Sri Lanka approached replacement fertility, Nepal continued to add substantial absolute numbers.

3. Demographic maturation and decelerating momentum (2011 to 2026): Regional population expanded from 47,8M to 54,5M, with annual growth dropping below 0,89%. Below-replacement fertility in Sri Lanka, sub-replacement fertility across urban Nepal and massive overseas migration moderated domestic expansion.

## Sub-Regional Analysis and Differential Growth Regimes

### Central and Eastern Nepal

Central and Eastern Nepal maintained the largest demographic mass among the six sub-regions, expanding from 5,44M in 1947 to 10,94M in 1981 and 19,62M by 2026 across 66.543 km². Sub-regional density rose from 81,7 to 294,8 persons per km².

Growth was propelled by two engines: the agricultural boom in the eastern Tarai (Morang, Sunsari, Jhapa, Dhanusha, Sarlahi) and the urban agglomerations of the Kathmandu and Pokhara valleys [@Slusser1982NepalMandala; @Prachhai2025Demograp].

Kathmandu expanded from 106,6k in 1952 to a municipal peak of 975.453 in 2011AD (862,4k in 2021 and 910k in 2025), merging with Lalitpur (315k peak in 2025AD) and Bhaktapur into a continuous valley conurbation. Further west in Gandaki, Pokhara grew from 12k in 1961 to 550k (550.000) by 2025AD as a premier tourism, aviation and regional service hub, while Bharatpur (390.501 peak in 2025AD) anchored the Chitwan valley.

Secondary industrial centres along the Indian border also underwent substantial nucleation, notably Birgunj (290k peak in 2025AD) as the primary transit port for foreign imports and Biratnagar (258k peak in 2025AD) as an early manufacturing hub, alongside Dharan (141,1k), Lahan (125,1k), Janakpurdham (118,8k) and Hetauda (102,9k).

### Western Nepal

Western Nepal expanded from 2,87M in 1947 to 5,78M in 1981 and 10,36M by 2026 across 78.465 km², with density rising from 36,6 to 132 persons per km².

This sub-region exhibits marked internal divergence. While the mountainous Karnali province remained sparsely populated and suffered chronic seasonal out-migration, the southern plains of Lumbini and Sudurpashchim experienced rapid post-malaria growth [@Sharma2026Internal].

In the southern plains, Ghorahi (189,7k peak in 2025AD), Butwal (143,9k), Bhimdatta (127,1k), Dhangadhi (123,9k) and Nepalgunj (88,1k) grew into vital agro-commercial conduits along the Indian border, transforming former forest tracts into dense market settlements.

### Sri Lanka (Wet and South)

The southwestern and central provinces of Sri Lanka supported 5,59M inhabitants in 1947, expanding to 11,25M in 1981 and 20,16M by 2026 across 45.939 km². Population density reached 438,9 persons per km² by 2026, the highest among the continental sub-regions.

Urbanisation in this zone assumed an extended peri-urban form: rather than concentrating exclusively within the municipal boundary of Colombo (645k peak in 2025AD), population coalesced along an 80-kilometre coastal ribbon encompassing Dehiwala-Mount Lavinia (247.973 in 2025AD), Maharagama (234,1k), Moratuwa (201,6k), Beruwala (197,7k), Gampaha (191k) and Negombo (170,3k) [@Abeykoon2000Fertilit].

The plantation districts of the central highlands around Kandy (112k in 2025AD), Nuwara Eliya and Badulla accommodated significant communities of Tamil estate workers, whose fertility converged with national norms during the late twentieth century.

The southern littoral around Galle (96k) and Matara (91,4k) maintained steady fishing and commercial activity while feeding domestic migration to the capital district.

### Sri Lanka (North and East)

The Northern and Eastern provinces expanded from 831k in 1947 to 1,67M in 1981 and 3M by 2026 across 17.754 km², with density increasing from 46,8 to 168,8 persons per km².

Demographic growth in this sub-region was severely punctuated by the 1983-2009 conflict, which triggered substantial refugee movements to Tamil Nadu, large-scale diaspora emigration to Europe and North America, and internal displacement within the Vanni [@Maric2025Changes].

On the northern peninsula, Jaffna reached a pre-conflict peak of 118,2k in 1981AD before war-related displacement lowered its municipal count to 88,1k in 2001 and 2012, followed by gradual recovery to 100k by 2025AD. Along the eastern coast, Kalmunai (120k), Trincomalee (118,8k) and Batticaloa (103,9k) maintained steady regional growth, though overall expansion remained slower than in the southwest owing to lower natural increase and continued youth out-migration.

### Kingdom of Bhutan

Bhutan expanded from 226,5k in 1947 to 456k in 1981 and 817,5k by 2026 across 38.704 km², maintaining the lowest population density in South Asia at 21,1 persons per km² in 2026.

Prior to the 1960s, settlement was almost entirely rural, organised around fortified monasteries and agricultural hamlets [@Phuntsho2013HistoryBhutan]. Modern planned urbanisation commenced with the establishment of Thimphu as the permanent capital in 1955.

Thimphu grew from 12k in 1961 to 114,6k in 2017 and 132k by 2025AD, anchoring modern civil administration, higher education and commercial services.

The southern border gateway of Phuntsholing (30,9k) emerged as the primary industrial and commercial entrepôt connecting Bhutan to the Indian transport grid, handling over 70% of national import and export cargo [@Paricha2016Economic].

Other dzongkhag centres such as Tsirang (25k), Punakha (24k), Pemagatshel (15,5k) and Paro (12,8k) retained compact populations serving administrative and ecclesiastical functions.

### Republic of Maldives

The Maldives expanded from 151k in 1947 to 304k in 1981 and 545k by 2026. While the physical land area of the archipelago is minimal (25 km² in 5-arcminute raster cells), the population distribution underwent unprecedented hyper-nucleation.

In 1965, the capital island of Malé housed 10,9k inhabitants. As international tourism, public hospital care and secondary schooling expanded from the 1970s onwards, atoll residents migrated en masse to the capital.

By 2025AD, Malé concentrated 228k inhabitants (211,9k in 2022) on an island of barely 2 km², producing an extraordinary local density exceeding 110.000 persons per km² and prompting state reclamation at Hulhumalé (5,2k registered residents by 2025AD) to alleviate severe spatial crowding.

Outer atoll communities on Fuvahmulah (11,6k), Hithadhoo in Addu City (10,4k) and Kulhudhuffushi (9,9k) developed secondary municipal functions, though Malé retained absolute dominance over tertiary employment and government services.

Settlement rank-size regression across the 4.523 catalogued localities yields a Pareto exponent of $\alpha = 0{,}68$ ($R^2 = 0{,}89$).

This shallow rank-size slope reflects the combination of primate capitals (Kathmandu and Colombo) with broad, densely populated hierarchies of intermediate market towns and agrarian *qasba* nodes across the Tarai, western Nepal and southwestern Sri Lanka.

# Limitations

## Census Gaps and Boundary Adjustments

Historical demographic reconstructions across post-colonial South Asia are subject to specific documentation constraints.

In Nepal, the progressive conversion of Village Development Committees (VDCs) into urban municipalities during the 2010s amalgamated rural tracts into nominal urban entities, creating artificial jumps in census urban shares that require careful boundary standardisation [@Prachhai2025Demograp].

## Conflict Disruptions and Enumeration Gaps

The civil conflict in Sri Lanka prevented full census enumeration in Jaffna, Kilinochchi, Mullaitivu and Mannar during the 2001 census round.

While administrative registries and displacement tallies enable reliable interpolation, localised settlement populations during the late 1990s carry wider uncertainty intervals than peacetime counts [@Maric2025Changes].

In Nepal, the 1996-2006 Maoist insurgency likewise suppressed enumerator access in remote highlands of Rolpa and Rukum, resulting in slight under-registration of migrant youth cohorts [@Channon2021Prevalen].

## Micro-Insular and Montane Under-Reporting

In the Maldives, temporary worker populations, comprising expatriate resort workers from Bangladesh, India and Sri Lanka living on non-administrative resort islands, are partially excluded from standard resident atoll censuses, leading to slight discrepancies between de jure and de facto resident totals.

In Bhutan, the exclusion of non-registered southern residents during early census rounds created demographic baseline adjustments that were only fully harmonised in the 2005 national census [@Paricha2016Economic].

# Conclusion

The post-independence demographic history of Nepal, Sri Lanka, Bhutan and the Maldives demonstrates how shared public health innovations produced highly divergent population trajectories across distinct geographical environments.

Between 1947 and 2026, the aggregate regional population expanded from 15,1M to 54,5M inhabitants.

Sri Lanka led the epidemiological and fertility transitions, transitioning from rapid post-malaria expansion to demographic stabilisation and population ageing.

Nepal underwent massive southward demographic reallocation, clearing the malarial Tarai to create a dynamic agrarian and urban frontier.

In Bhutan and the Maldives, modernisation transformed isolated mountain communities and coral atolls into urbanised state economies centred on Thimphu and Malé.

By integrating 4.523 catalogued settlement trajectories with sub-regional census series across eight decades, this reconstruction establishes a systematic spatial foundation for comparative demographic analysis, isolating nucleated urban centres from rural populations and tracing the emergence of modern urban hierarchies across South Asia northern and maritime frontiers.
